warmup.q: A team trains a fraud model on October's payments. Each payment is joined to one number about its card: "chargebacks in the last 30 days". (A chargeback is the bank taking a payment's money back after the cardholder says "that wasn't me".) They use each card's newest value of that number. On this training data, a simple rule catches 98% of fraud. What should they expect when the rule runs on new payments at the till?
options: Clearly less: the newest values counted chargebacks caused by the very payments it learned from, which the till never sees in time
More than 98%, because live payments bring more data
It depends only on which kind of model they train
warmup.why: The newest value was worked out after the month ended. For a fraudulent payment, it already counts the chargeback that this payment itself caused a few days later. So the rule learned to spot fraud by its own consequence. At the till, at the moment of the payment, that chargeback doesn't exist yet. In this lesson's demo, the same rule catches 98% on the leaky training data and 62% on honest training data, and 62% is what the till gets. The third option is the trap: more data doesn't help a rule that learned from the future.

sections.h: Getting data in shape: from ETL to ELT, and what dbt does
sections.html:
The nightly jobs of the last lesson left a fresh table behind every morning: the day's totals for each shop. Every batch job in this track ends like that, with a new output. Who reads it? There are four common homes: tables reshaped for analysts, reports and running totals, training data for machine learning, and data a live app reads. (Analysts are people whose job is answering questions with data.) The first two get data into shape. The last two send it back into the live system, and that's where most of the mistakes happen.

Start with getting data in shape. The payments company keeps its data in several places, each built for its own daily work. Payments live in the app's main database. The shops' details live in the database of the program that signs new shops up. Complaints about payments live in a tool bought from another company. The warehouse from Warehouses and dimensional models: OLAP and star schemas needs all of it cleaned, reshaped and joined. Joining means matching up rows from different places, such as each payment with its shop. It wants facts, one row per event such as a payment, and dimensions, one row per thing such as a shop.

Version 1 is ETL: extract the data from each system, transform it on separate servers, then load the result into the warehouse. (A server is a computer that runs programs for others.) The transform came first because warehouse computing was expensive. A warehouse was often an appliance, one big machine bought with a fixed amount of power and shared by everyone, so only finished data went in.

ETL breaks on change. A new question needs a field the transform dropped. An engineer has to change the job that feeds the warehouse and reload, and the raw data that would have answered the question is gone. The Lakehouse paper, given at the CIDR database conference in 2021, cites a survey on this. 86% of analysts said they used out-of-date data, and 62% said they waited for engineers several times a month.

Version 2 is ELT: load the raw data first, as it is, into the lake or the warehouse, and transform it there afterwards, with SQL. (A lake is plain files on cheap cloud storage. A lakehouse adds tables on top of those files, as in Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg.) It became possible when cloud warehouses and lakehouses made storage cheap and computing elastic, meaning you rent as much as a job needs for as long as it runs. Keeping every raw column costs little, and a new transform runs whenever someone needs it.

The tool most teams use for the T, the transform step, is dbt, a free program for managing SQL transforms. Each transform is a file holding one SELECT query, called a model. A model names the models it reads with ref('stg_payments'). From those references, dbt builds a DAG of models, the same kind of graph as in Orchestrating batch work, and runs them in order. It turns each SELECT into a table, a view (a saved query), or an incremental MERGE that adds only what's new, and the warehouse does the work. dbt also runs tests after each build, such as unique, not_null, and checks that each payment's shop exists. It moves no data itself. Getting the raw tables in is another tool's job, such as Fivetran, Airbyte, Kafka Connect or Spark. dbt-core 1.12 is current.

Data teams also make the trip back, called reverse ETL: pushing warehouse results into the tools staff use every day, such as the sales team's list of customers.

The analytics outputs are ones you've met: the star schemas of the warehouse lesson, and the summary tables and data cubes of Materialized views and data cubes. Both are refreshed on a schedule. Some go into a real-time analytics database such as Druid or Pinot, built to answer dashboard questions fast. The rest of this lesson follows the outputs that a running system reads, starting with the model behind the bank's text.

sections.h: Training data that can't see the future: the point-in-time join
sections.html:
A fraud model learns from labels: past payments, each marked fraud or not. The mark comes weeks later, once a chargeback arrives or doesn't. A chargeback is the bank taking a payment's money back from the shop after the cardholder says "I didn't make this payment". The model learns from features too: numbers about each payment's card and shop, such as "chargebacks on this card in the last 30 days". At the till, the model sees each feature as it is at that moment. So the training data must show it each feature as it was at each label's moment, too.

A railway timetable makes the rule easy to see. Say a passenger complains that she missed her connection at 14:00 last Tuesday. To judge whether she picked a sensible train, you'd look at the timetable that was on the board that Tuesday, not today's. Today's board knows about changes she couldn't have seen.

Version 1 joins every label to the feature table as it is now: one row per card, holding the newest value. It's the easy join, and it's wrong in a way no test catches. Take a fraudulent payment on 10 October. It caused a chargeback on 12 October, which the nightly feature job counted from 13 October on. So the card's newest row says 1. Joined to the 10 October label, it tells the model that fraud comes with a chargeback already on file. That's true only because the fraud itself caused it.

This is label leakage: facts from after the decision reaching the data the model learns from. In the Try it, one simple rule catches 98% of fraud on the leaky training data and 62% on the honest one. 62% is what the till gets.

Version 2 is a point-in-time join. For a label at time t, take the feature row whose time is the newest one at or before t. That fixes the leak above, but it misses a second one. A feature row has two times. One is the moment the value is about, asOf: midnight, for a nightly job. The other is the moment it was written, computedAt: 02:00 that night, or days later for a correction or a backfill. A payment at 01:00 on 13 October couldn't have seen the 13 October row, written at 02:00. And a correction of 12 October, written on 15 October, didn't exist for any payment before 15 October.

So the rule has three parts. Take the newest row whose asOf is at or before t, and whose computedAt is at or before t too. Ignore rows older than a time-to-live (TTL), a limit after which a value counts as missing. The stepper applies the rule to one card.

Train only on what the model could have read at that moment. Anything written later doesn't count.

Feature stores, programs that keep features for models, do this for you. Feast, a free one, scans backward from each label's time up to the feature's TTL, using each row's event time, our asOf, by default. Its documentation describes filter_by_created_timestamp=True, which also requires that the value was written by then, to keep backfilled values out of training data. Some SQL engines have it as a join type. DuckDB, a database that runs inside one program on one machine, has ASOF JOIN, which matches each row to the nearest earlier one. Spark 4.3 added ASOF JOIN too, behind a setting that's off by default.

A feature store also keeps two copies of each feature, filled by the same code. An offline store holds the history in lakehouse tables, for training and backfills. An online store holds the latest values in a key-value store, a database that looks up one value by its key, fast, for the model at the till. Getting a night's fresh values into a store like that is the next section's problem.

try.title: Score a rule on leaky and honest training data
steps: From the labs folder, run PointInTimeDemo. It makes up a month of payments on 5,000 cards, 5% of them stolen at some point, and the nightly chargeback feature. It builds the training data twice and scores the rule "flag the payment if the card has had a chargeback" on each.
Before you read: which training data makes the rule look better, and on which measure?
Why do the last two lines agree exactly?

code.title: PointInTimeDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l14.demo import java.time.Duration import java.time.Instant import kotlin.random.Random /** * A month of card payments with fraud labels, and the feature "chargebacks on this card in the * last 30 days", computed every night. The training set is built twice: once with each card's * newest feature value, once point in time. Then a one-line rule, "flag the payment if the card * has had a chargeback", is scored on both, and on what it would really see in production. */ private data class Label(val card: Int, val at: Instant, val fraud: Boolean) private data class Row(val card: Int, val asOf: Instant, val computedAt: Instant, val value: Int) fun main() { val start = Instant.parse("2026-10-01T00:00:00Z") val rnd = Random(11) val labels = mutableListOf<Label>() val chargebacks = mutableListOf<Pair<Int, Instant>>() for (card in 0 until 5_000) { val compromisedFrom = if (rnd.nextDouble() < 0.05) 3 + rnd.nextInt(24) else Int.MAX_VALUE for (d in 0 until 30) { val at = start.plus(Duration.ofDays(d.toLong())).plusSeconds(rnd.nextLong(86_400)) val fraud = d >= compromisedFrom && rnd.nextDouble() < 0.6 labels += Label(card, at, fraud) if (fraud) chargebacks += card to at.plus(Duration.ofHours(48 + rnd.nextLong(144))) else if (rnd.nextDouble() < 0.003) chargebacks += card to at.plus(Duration.ofHours(120 + rnd.nextLong(360))) } } val byCard = chargebacks.groupBy({ it.first }, { it.second }) val rows = (0 until 5_000).flatMap { card -> (0..30).map { d -> val asOf = start.plus(Duration.ofDays(d.toLong())) Row(card, asOf, asOf.plus(Duration.ofHours(2)), byCard[card].orEmpty().count { it < asOf && it >= asOf.minus(Duration.ofDays(30)) }) } } val history = rows.groupBy { it.card }.mapValues { (_, r) -> r.sortedBy { it.asOf } } val newest = labels.map { l -> l to history.getValue(l.card).last() } val pointInTime = labels.map { l -> l to history.getValue(l.card).lastOrNull { it.asOf <= l.at && it.computedAt <= l.at } } println("labels: %,d payments, %,d of them fraud; feature rows: %,d".format(labels.size, labels.count { it.fraud }, rows.size)) println("newest-row join: %,d labels got a value computed after the payment".format(newest.count { (l, r) -> r.computedAt > l.at })) println("point-in-time join: %,d".format(pointInTime.count { (l, r) -> r != null && r.computedAt > l.at })) fun score(name: String, set: List<Pair<Label, Row?>>) { val flagged = set.filter { (_, r) -> (r?.value ?: 0) >= 1 } val caught = flagged.count { it.first.fraud } println("%-38s flags %,6d payments: precision %3.0f%%, recall %3.0f%%".format(name, flagged.size, 100.0 * caught / flagged.size, 100.0 * caught / labels.count { it.fraud })) } println("the rule \"the card has had a chargeback in the last 30 days\":") score(" trained on the newest-row join", newest) score(" trained on the point-in-time join", pointInTime) score(" in production (what it can see live)", pointInTime) }

try.expect:
labels: 150,000 payments, 2,378 of them fraud; feature rows: 155,000
newest-row join:    150,000 labels got a value computed after the payment
point-in-time join: 0
the rule "the card has had a chargeback in the last 30 days":
  trained on the newest-row join       flags 15,000 payments: precision  16%, recall  98%
  trained on the point-in-time join    flags  4,690 payments: precision  31%, recall  62%
  in production (what it can see live) flags  4,690 payments: precision  31%, recall  62%

The newest feature row for every card is the one written after the month ended, so all 150,000 labels got a value from their future. On that leaky data, the rule seems to catch 98% of fraud. That's recall, the share of all fraud the rule flags, and it's high because nearly every fraud's own chargeback is already in its feature. On the point-in-time data it catches 62%, because a stolen card's first fraudulent payments happen before any chargeback exists. Precision, the share of flagged payments that really are fraud, even looks worse on the leaky data (16% against 31%), because it flags every payment of every card that had a chargeback by the end of the month. At the till, the model reads exactly what the point-in-time join gave it, which is why the last two lines match. Only the honest training data predicts what the live rule will do. The data comes from a fixed seed, so you get the same numbers.

sections.h: Handing a night's results to a live app, without writing row by row
sections.html:
Tonight's batch job has given each of 1,000,000 shops a risk score, a number for how likely its payments are to go wrong. The program that approves payments at the till needs the new scores by morning. The tempting design: each task of the job writes its rows straight into the live database as it goes. It sends one row at a time, with UPDATE merchant_risk SET score = ? WHERE merchant_id = ?.

It breaks three ways. The first is speed. One round trip to a database, a request and its answer over the network, costs a millisecond or two from the machines running a batch job. Take 2 ms, a pool of 20 connections (open links to the database that the job shares), and a bigger night: 50 million card scores. 50,000,000 / 20 x 2 ms is 5,000 seconds, almost an hour and a half of the database's time, while live payments compete with the batch writes. Give the job 200 tasks with their own connections, and it can take the database down.

The second is what readers see. While the job runs, half the rows hold tonight's scores and half hold yesterday's. A program that reads several of them gets a mix that no run ever produced. In the Try it, a reader caught 568 new and 432 old scores in one sample. Back at the railway station, it's someone walking along the platforms crossing out departure times one by one while passengers read the boards. Halfway through, a passenger changing trains reads one old board and one new one.

The third is failure. Orchestrating batch work made each job's output appear in one step, all or nothing. These writes don't. A job that dies halfway leaves half the table updated, and its retry writes everything again.

There are two better designs. The first publishes through a log. The job writes its output to a topic, a named log, in Kafka, a program that keeps ordered logs of messages for other programs to read at their own pace. Elasticsearch, Pinot, Druid, Venice and ClickHouse, all stores built for fast reads, can load from Kafka. The log absorbs the burst, and several stores can read the same output. All or nothing still needs one more message: a "run complete" marker, with readers keeping the new run out of sight until it arrives.

The second builds the whole store inside the batch job, as files, and hands the files over at once: a bulk load. At the station, it's printing the whole new timetable in the back office and putting it up in one go. RocksDB, a storage engine (the part of a database that keeps data on disk) from LSM trees, SSTables and Bloom filters, has a way to do exactly this. Normally each write to RocksDB goes to a log on disk and to a sorted table in memory, the memtable. Later it's written out to a sorted file, an SST file, and merged with other files again and again, which is called compaction.

A bulk load skips all of that. SstFileWriter writes a sorted SST file outside the database, and it accepts keys only in strictly increasing order. IngestExternalFile then copies or links the file into the database. It pauses writes for a moment to give the whole file one sequence number, the counter RocksDB uses to order writes. It writes the memtable out first if their keys overlap. RocksDB keeps its files in a stack of levels, and compaction moves data down them. The new file goes into the lowest level where its keys overlap nothing, and writes go on. The data skips the log, the memtable and every compaction that a million single writes would have caused.

Google built its web search index the same way. It used 5 to 10 passes of MapReduce, its system for one job spread over thousands of machines, over more than 20 TB of web pages. Pinot's data files can be built like this in a job on Hadoop or Spark, the two big batch systems of this track. TiDB Lightning, the import tool of the TiDB database, works this way too. In the Try it, writing a sorted file of 1,000,000 scores took 67 ms, and nobody could see it until it was finished. Next, we'll make the last step, the switch, safe.

try.title: Update a live store in place, or build and switch
steps: From the labs folder, run BulkLoadDemo. It overwrites 1,000,000 shop scores in a live map (a lookup table in memory) one by one, while a reader samples 1,000 of them every 20 ms. Then it writes the same scores as a sorted file in a new folder and switches a pointer to it.
Predict what the reader sees halfway through the in-place update.
What would change if each in-place write were a 2 ms database round trip instead of a map update?

code.title: BulkLoadDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l14.demo import java.io.File import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import kotlin.concurrent.thread import kotlin.random.Random /** * Last night's batch job scored 1,000,000 merchants again. Two ways to get the new scores to the * service that reads them: write them one by one into the live store while it serves, or build a * new read-only file offline and switch to it in one step. A reader samples 1,000 merchants while * each runs. */ fun main() { val n = 1_000_000 val keys = Array(n) { "merchant-%07d".format(it) } val pick = Random(1) val sample = (0 until 1_000).map { keys[pick.nextInt(n)] } // 1. row by row into the live store, in the order the job's tasks happen to finish val live = ConcurrentHashMap<String, String>(n * 2) keys.forEach { live[it] = "run-1" } val seen = mutableListOf<Int>() val writing = AtomicBoolean(true) val reader = thread { while (writing.get()) { seen += sample.count { live[it] == "run-2" } Thread.sleep(20) } } val t0 = System.nanoTime() for (i in keys.indices.shuffled(Random(2))) live[keys[i]] = "run-2" writing.set(false) reader.join() val inPlaceMs = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1e6 val mixed = seen.filter { it in 1..999 } println("in place: %,d writes in %.0f ms; the reader looked %d times while it ran, and %d of those reads mixed both runs".format( n, inPlaceMs, seen.size, mixed.size)) if (mixed.isNotEmpty()) println(" for example, %d of the 1,000 sampled merchants had new scores and %d still had old ones".format(mixed[mixed.size / 2], 1_000 - mixed[mixed.size / 2])) // 2. offline: write a sorted file in a new folder, then flip a pointer val root = File("build/l14/scores").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } val t1 = System.nanoTime() val v2 = File(root, "v2").apply { mkdirs() } File(v2, "data").bufferedWriter().use { w -> for (k in keys.sorted()) { w.write(k); w.write("\trun-2\n") } } val buildMs = (System.nanoTime() - t1) / 1e6 val tmp = File(root, "CURRENT.tmp").apply { writeText("v2") } val t2 = System.nanoTime() Files.move(tmp.toPath(), File(root, "CURRENT").toPath(), StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING) val swapUs = (System.nanoTime() - t2) / 1e3 println("offline: built a sorted file of %,d entries (%.1f MB) in %.0f ms, which no reader could see;".format( n, File(v2, "data").length() / 1e6, buildMs)) println(" then the switch took %.0f microseconds: a reader sees run 1 or run 2, never both".format(swapUs)) }

try.expect:
in place: 1,000,000 writes in 226 ms; the reader looked 8 times while it ran, and 6 of those reads mixed both runs
  for example, 568 of the 1,000 sampled merchants had new scores and 432 still had old ones
offline: built a sorted file of 1,000,000 entries (23.0 MB) in 67 ms, which no reader could see;
  then the switch took 720 microseconds: a reader sees run 1 or run 2, never both

The in-place writes here go to a map in memory, which is far faster than a database over a network: 226 ms for a million writes instead of an hour. Even so, most of the reader's samples mixed two runs of the model. With a real database, the mixed window lasts as long as the whole load. The offline build wrote a sorted file nobody could read until it was done, and switching to it was one rename. Times vary with your computer. The mixed reads come from the timing of two threads (two lines of work running at once in one program), so your counts will differ.

aside.title: Couldn't the job write every row inside one transaction?
aside.html: It would fix the mix: readers keep seeing last night's scores until the commit, and a crash undoes everything. It doesn't fix the speed. Every row is still a round trip, so the transaction stays open for over an hour. All that time it holds a lock on every row it changed, so anything else that wants to change those rows waits, and the database keeps the old copy of each row until the end. And a failure in the 59th minute throws the whole hour away.

sections.h: Publishing a new version in one step, and rolling back in one more
sections.html:
A store built in bulk still has to replace yesterday's. Copying the new file over the old one in place brings back both problems of the last section. A reader during the copy reads half of each, and a crash in the middle leaves a broken store. The fix is the one this track keeps coming back to.

Never change a published output. An output that never changes is called immutable. Each run writes a new version in a new place: v41/, v42/, v43/. Nobody reads a version until it's complete. One small thing that does change, a pointer, names the live version. It can be a file called CURRENT that holds the version's name. It can also be a symbolic link (a file that stands for another file) or a row in a catalog (a list of tables and where their files are). In a search engine, it's an alias. Publishing a version means replacing that pointer in one atomic step, one that happens whole or not at all.

On one file system, that step is a rename: write CURRENT.tmp, then rename it over CURRENT. POSIX, the standard that Linux and macOS follow for files, says rename replaces the target in one step. So every reader finds either the old name or the new one, never a missing or half-written file. A reader reads the pointer once, then opens that version and keeps it for the whole request.

You get three things for free.

  • A crashed build is a folder nobody points at. The live version keeps serving, and the folder is deleted later.
  • A bad build is one publish away from being undone: publish the previous version again. It was never changed, so rolling back is instant and exact.
  • Clean-up is safe by rule: delete only versions that nothing points at and no reader still holds.

Never change a published version. Build the next one beside it, and move the pointer.

At the station, this is the old timetable kept in the drawer. If the new one has a mistake, the staff put the old one back up. The picture breaks at the swap itself. A station needs a night and a crew to change every board, while a rename takes microseconds, and every reader sees it at the same instant.

You've met this design before. An Iceberg commit (Lakehouse tables with Apache Iceberg) writes new files where no reader looks. Then it swaps the table's pointer with a compare-and-swap, a change that succeeds only if the pointer still holds what the writer read. RocksDB keeps its own CURRENT file, naming its live list of files. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch, two search engines, let you move an alias, a second name, from the old index (their word for a table) to the new one in one request. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, a well-known book on these systems, calls the batch half of the idea human fault tolerance. If the output is wrong, fix the code and run again, because the old output was never destroyed. The pointer swap brings that to the live app.

In the Try it, night 1 publishes v1. Night 2's build crashes after 400 of 1,000 lines, and readers never notice. Night 3 publishes v3 with a bug that sets every score to 0, and the rollback to v1 is a single publish.

The design has a limit. Every version is a whole new copy, so changing ten shops' scores still means building and shipping all million. And the live app is only as fresh as the last build. A store that takes a bulk version each night and single updates in between needs more machinery; Go deeper names one.

try.title: Three nights of builds: a good one, a crash and a bad one
steps: From the labs folder, run SwapDemo. Night 1 builds and publishes v1. Night 2's build dies after 400 lines. Night 3 publishes v3, which has a bug, and then v1 is published again.
After night 2, predict what a reader gets for merchant 42, the shop it looks up.
List the folders at the end. Which can a clean-up job delete right now?

code.title: SwapDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l14.demo import java.io.File import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption /** * Three nights of a serving store built by a batch job: a good build, a build that crashes * halfway, and a build with bad scores that is published and then rolled back. Prints the folder * and what a reader gets after each step. */ fun main() { val root = File("build/l14/store").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } val current = File(root, "CURRENT") fun publish(v: String) { val tmp = File(root, "CURRENT.tmp").apply { writeText(v) } Files.move(tmp.toPath(), current.toPath(), StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING) } fun build(v: String, score: Int, crashAfter: Int = Int.MAX_VALUE) { val dir = File(root, v).apply { mkdirs() } File(dir, "data").bufferedWriter().use { w -> for (m in 0 until 1_000) { if (m == crashAfter) throw IllegalStateException("executor lost while writing $v") w.write("merchant-%04d\t$score\n".format(m)) } } } fun read(): String { val v = current.readText() val line = File(root, "$v/data").readLines().first { it.startsWith("merchant-0042\t") } return "CURRENT=$v, merchant-0042 scores ${line.substringAfter('\t')}" } fun show(step: String) { val folders = root.list()!!.filter { it.startsWith("v") }.sorted().joinToString { v -> "$v (${File(root, "$v/data").readLines().size} lines)" } println("$step\n folders: $folders\n a reader: ${read()}") } build("v1", 17); publish("v1"); show("night 1: build v1, publish") runCatching { build("v2", 18, crashAfter = 400) }.onFailure { println("night 2: the build failed: ${it.message}") } show(" nothing was published") build("v3", 0); publish("v3"); show("night 3: build v3 with a bug (every score 0), publish") publish("v1"); show("rollback: publish v1 again") }

try.expect:
night 1: build v1, publish
  folders: v1 (1000 lines)
  a reader: CURRENT=v1, merchant-0042 scores 17
night 2: the build failed: executor lost while writing v2
  nothing was published
  folders: v1 (1000 lines), v2 (400 lines)
  a reader: CURRENT=v1, merchant-0042 scores 17
night 3: build v3 with a bug (every score 0), publish
  folders: v1 (1000 lines), v2 (400 lines), v3 (1000 lines)
  a reader: CURRENT=v3, merchant-0042 scores 0
rollback: publish v1 again
  folders: v1 (1000 lines), v2 (400 lines), v3 (1000 lines)
  a reader: CURRENT=v1, merchant-0042 scores 17

The failed build left a 400-line v2 that no pointer names, so readers kept getting v1, and nothing had to be repaired. The buggy v3 went live, as bad builds sometimes do, and undoing it was one more publish of v1, which nobody had touched. A clean-up job would now delete v2 and, once nobody reads it, v3. The folders are under labs/sim/build/l14/store if you want to look.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 11: serving derived data

mistake: The common mistake is building training data with a plain join to the current feature table, because that's the table that exists and the join is one line. Nothing fails. The model trains, its scores on old payments look excellent, and it does worse live for reasons nobody can find, because the training rows held facts from after each decision. The leak hides even better when it comes from a backfill or a correction, which have an old asOf and a new computedAt. The fix is to keep feature history with both times and to join point in time: the newest row whose two times are both at or before the label's time, within a TTL. Use your feature store's history lookup or a SQL ASOF or LATERAL join. Then add a check to the pipeline that counts rows whose feature was written after their label.
opening:
Your bank sends you a text: "Was this you? 300.00 at a shop in Lisbon." Behind it is a program that learned from past payments which ones turned out to be fraud, payments made with a stolen card. Picture the team that built one. Trained and scored on last month's payments, it caught 98% of the fraud. Then they switched it on, and it caught 62%.

Nothing in the code was wrong. The training data joined each old payment to the facts about its card as they stand today. That felt honest, because every fact was real history. But some of those facts happened after the payment, and the model learned from them.

Orchestrating batch work: DAGs, retries and backfills made each nightly job safe to run twice, but where does its output go? In this lesson, we'll follow batch output to its four homes. We'll build training data that can't see the future, and hand a million new scores to a live app in one step. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a fraud model that caught 98% of fraud on old payments and 62% at the till. Its training data had joined each payment to its card's newest numbers, which already counted the chargebacks the fraud caused. Joining each payment to what existed at its own moment shows the 62% before the model goes live.

After the last Try it, look in labs/sim/build/l14/store and run cat CURRENT. It names the live version, and the folders beside it are every build, the crashed one included.

Next, we'll choose the engine that runs all this work. Is it one laptop or a cluster of machines, and how can you tell with numbers before you choose?

compare.title: Getting tonight's scores to the live app

a.label: Row by row into the live database
a.title: each task writes as it goes
a.html: scores.foreachPartition { rows -> pool.connection.use { c -> val ps = c.prepareStatement("UPDATE merchant_risk SET score = ? WHERE merchant_id = ?") rows.forEach { r -> ps.setDouble(1, r.score); ps.setLong(2, r.merchantId) ps.executeUpdate() // one round trip per row, visible at once } } }

b.label: Build offline, then switch
b.title: one new version, one pointer flip
b.html: val version = "v$runId" scores.orderBy("merchant_id").write().parquet("$root/$version") // nobody reads it yet check(spark.read().parquet("$root/$version").count() == expected) val tmp = Files.writeString(Path.of(root, "CURRENT.tmp"), version) Files.move(tmp, Path.of(root, "CURRENT"), ATOMIC_MOVE) // every reader switches at once // rollback: publish the previous version again

compare.note: The left side spends one database round trip per row, competes with live payments for the whole load, shows readers a mix of two runs, and leaves half the table updated if the job dies. The right side writes files in order where nobody reads them, can be checked before anyone sees them, and becomes visible in one step that is also its rollback. The Files.move with ATOMIC_MOVE on the right is the publish the lab builds.

worked.title: Ship tonight's shop risk scores as a RocksDB snapshot

steps.say: Work out the scores as of the run's logical date (the day of data the run is for), so a rerun produces the same file. Sort by key: an SST file accepts keys only in strictly increasing order, and sorting is cheap inside the batch job.
steps.code: val scores = spark.table("features.merchant_daily") .where(col("as_of").equalTo(lit(logicalDate))) .select(col("merchant_id"), scoreExpression.alias("score")) .orderBy("merchant_id")

steps.say: Write the sorted rows into an SST file with SstFileWriter from RocksJava, RocksDB's library for Java and Kotlin. finish() writes the file's index and footer; until then, the file isn't a valid table.
steps.code: // key(): the id as 8 big-endian bytes, so byte order is numeric order; value(): the score as bytes Options().use { opts -> SstFileWriter(EnvOptions(), opts).use { w -> w.open("$root/v$runId/scores.sst") for (row in scores.toLocalIterator()) { w.put(key(row.getLong(0)), value(row.getDouble(1))) // keys must strictly increase } w.finish() } }

steps.say: Load it into a fresh database folder for this version. RocksDB places the file straight into its levels of files, with no log, memtable or compaction for its data.
steps.code: RocksDB.open(Options().setCreateIfMissing(true), "$root/v$runId/db").use { db -> IngestExternalFileOptions().use { io -> db.ingestExternalFile(listOf("$root/v$runId/scores.sst"), io) } }

steps.say: Check the new version before anyone reads it, then publish it by replacing the pointer in one step. The live app reads CURRENT on each request (or watches it for changes) and opens that version read-only.
steps.code: RocksDB.openReadOnly(Options(), "$root/v$runId/db").use { db -> check(knownMerchants.all { db.get(key(it)) != null }) // spot-check before anyone reads it } val tmp = Files.writeString(root.resolve("CURRENT.tmp"), "v$runId") Files.move(tmp, root.resolve("CURRENT"), StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE)

steps.say: Keep the previous version until the new one has served a full day. If the scores turn out wrong, rolling back is the same publish with the old name. Delete versions only when nothing points at them.
steps.code: publish("v${runId - 1}") // rollback deleteVersionsOlderThan(keep = 2) // clean-up, never the live one

lab.title: Training data without leaks, and a store you can swap
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail on TODOs. Read FraudData.kt: the labels, the feature rows with both asOf and computedAt, the given latestJoin that leaks, and leaks, which counts rows whose feature didn't exist yet at the label's time.

Exercise 1, TrainingSet.pointInTimeJoin: for each label, the newest row of its card with asOf and computedAt both at or before the label's time, no older than the TTL. On a tie of asOf, take the later computedAt. PointInTimeTest checks hand-built cases first, then a month of data for 500 cards against a slow scan of every row.
Exercise 2, ServingStore.build: refuse duplicate keys before creating anything, then write the sorted entries to the next version folder. Never touch CURRENT.
Exercise 3, publish, current and open: write the version's name to a temporary file and move it over CURRENT with ATOMIC_MOVE. Read CURRENT once, and open that version's file.
Run until all eight pass. The last test runs three reader threads while 29 versions are published. A publish that deletes CURRENT first, or writes it in place, fails it sooner or later.
hints: Group the rows by card and sort each group with compareBy({ it.asOf }, { it.computedAt }). Binary-search (halve the range at each step) for the first row with asOf after the label, then walk back until a row has computedAt <= label.at. Stop when asOf is older than label.at.minus(ttl).
Next version: list root, keep names matching v\d+, and take one more than the highest (or v1). Check for duplicates on the sorted list: equal keys sit next to each other.

Files.createTempFile(root, "CURRENT", ".tmp"), Files.writeString(tmp, version), then Files.move(tmp, root.resolve("CURRENT"), StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING). Keep the temporary file in root: an atomic move only works within one file system.
lab.done: All eight tests in PointInTimeTest and ServingStoreTest pass.

drill.title: A point-in-time join in SQL
drill.prompt: From memory, write SQL that gives each row of labels(payment_id, card_id, at, fraud) the value from card_features(card_id, as_of, computed_at, value) that a model could have read at at. That's the newest row by as_of with both times at or before at, at most 2 days old, or NULL if there's none. (A LATERAL join, which runs a small query once for each row on its left, is one way to write it.)

answer.html: SELECT l.payment_id, l.fraud, f.value FROM labels l LEFT JOIN LATERAL ( SELECT value FROM card_features f WHERE f.card_id = l.card_id AND f.as_of <= l.at -- about the past AND f.computed_at <= l.at -- and already written then AND f.as_of >= l.at - INTERVAL '2 days' -- the TTL ORDER BY f.as_of DESC, f.computed_at DESC LIMIT 1 ) f ON true; -- DuckDB's ASOF JOIN matches on as_of alone (ON l.card_id = f.card_id AND l.at >= f.as_of); -- filter out rows written later than their label separately, or corrections will leak

recap: Batch output has four homes: tables reshaped for analysts, reports and running totals, training data for models, and data a live app reads. The last two feed the live system, and that's where most mistakes happen.

ETL transformed data before loading it, because warehouse computing was scarce. ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse with SQL. dbt manages those SQL models as a DAG with tests, and moves no data itself.

Training data must be point in time: each label gets the newest feature row whose asOf and computedAt are both at or before the label's time, within a TTL. A plain join to today's features leaks the future, and the model looks better on old data than it will ever be live.

Feature stores keep an offline history for training and an online store of latest values for the live model, filled by the same code. Feast, DuckDB's ASOF JOIN and Spark 4.3's ASOF JOIN do the point-in-time part.

Don't write batch output into a live database row by row: it costs a round trip per row, shows readers a mix of two runs, and leaves half a table on failure. Publish through Kafka with a "run complete" marker, or build the store offline, bulk-load it and move one pointer in one step. Rollback is moving it back.
The limit: every version is a whole new copy, so a small change still means a full rebuild, and the live app is only as fresh as the last build.

explain.prompt: Explain to a new teammate on the fraud team why the model caught 98% of fraud on old payments and 62% live, and what the training pipeline must do differently.
explain.answer: Each training row joins a payment, labelled fraud or not, to the card's feature "chargebacks in the last 30 days". The pipeline took each card's newest feature row, which was written after the whole month had ended. For a fraudulent payment, that row already counted the chargeback the fraud itself caused a few days later. So in training, frauds almost always came with a chargeback on file, and the rule learned to spot fraud by its own consequence. At the till, at the moment of the payment, that chargeback doesn't exist yet. So live, the rule only catches fraud on cards that already had an earlier chargeback: 62%. The fix is a point-in-time join. For each payment, take the newest feature row that was about a time at or before the payment and had really been written by then, within a TTL. Both conditions matter. The first stops future values; the second stops corrections and backfills that were written later about earlier days. That training data shows the model exactly what it will see live, so the score on old payments matches the live score. Feast's history lookup with the created-timestamp filter, or an ASOF or LATERAL join with both conditions, does it. The pipeline should also count rows whose feature was written after their label, and stop if there are any.

deeper.html:
Machine learning keeps batch busy beyond training data. Batch inference scores every shop or card overnight and serves the results through exactly the bulk load and swap of this lesson. Preparing data for large language models is a batch pipeline too: pull the text out of web pages, drop low-quality and duplicate documents, split the text into tokens and compute embeddings (lists of numbers that stand for meaning). Spark, Ray and purpose-built tools such as Kubeflow and Flyte run these jobs. Graph algorithms such as PageRank run as many rounds over the whole graph, called supersteps (the Pregel model).

Hybrid stores combine the two halves of this lesson. LinkedIn's Venice takes a bulk push of a whole new version each night and, between pushes, single-row updates from a stream. So a feature can be rebuilt from history in batch and kept fresh by streaming. Feature stores do the same with their offline and online stores. The hard part is keeping the code that fills both the same, or the model trains on one definition and is fed another.

Publishing through a log needs care at the reader. A reader that applies a run's records as they arrive shows a half-finished run, exactly like the row-by-row writer. It must collect the run out of sight and switch to it only on the "run complete" marker, much as the read committed isolation level hides changes that aren't committed yet. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition), chapter 11, covers ETL, analytics, machine learning and serving derived data as the four uses of batch output, and chapter 1 introduces data warehouses, lakes and ELT.
